doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Teaching jazz band setup: sax sections and seating
summary: He explains how to handle nine altos, section order, stacking leads, and alternatives like the Kenton Flying V.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That’s good. And your title is Curricular Jazz — do you teach people how to run a jazz band?
Well that’s important. Because for years, I mean almost every high school or junior high has a jazz band now. But a lot of teachers have no idea, like —

I have teachers calling me, people who’ve graduated, and they’ll call me and say, “um, I’m supposed to run this jazz ensemble and I’ve got nine alto players, what do I do?” And so I give them a little formula for doing that.

Don’t double the lead alto player. Double the second. Put an alto player with the baritone. That’s an octave apart. And you might have to transpose a tenor part, so you can do that. And then you get the full spread of sound. Even how to set up the saxophone section correctly. So it’s first alto, second alto, first tenor, second tenor, baritone. Because that’s the way the chord is voiced. And if you put two tenor players together then you get the kind of symphonic lag — how when you hear a stand partner to play —
Oh. Say that again. That’s interesting.

In symphony orchestras when you have two people on a stand invariably somebody is going to dominate. The other person could be a fraction behind. And often times they’ll wait for the stand partner to make the move. And this way if you have the tenor players, they’re not playing notes that clash up against each other, they’re spread down the line, they’re physically spread.

That’s interesting. Because we were discussing that this morning. “Well where do you want to sit? You want to put the tenors together?” And it’s not because I knew this thing, but I said, “well let’s not. Let’s put — you know. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -16-

And you stack the lead players. Trumpet, trombone and alto, kind of in the middle of the stage. And then you have the baritone and bass trombone together because often times they’re playing lines together. And the lead tenor player and second trumpet player are generally the soloists who’ll come out to the mics so they’re closest to the rhythm section.
Have you ever set the band up —
Oh you mean like the Kenton “Flying V?”

Yes I have. And in fact we’ve been rehearsing recently where the trumpets are facing this way, the trombones are facing this way, and the saxes facing the trumpets, just so that you can do it. I’ve also set them up where the trombones are in front, trumpets in the middle and the saxes in the back, which the Peter Herbolzheimer Band in Germany does that. So they have the saxes on a riser.
